    Last updated on 2026-10-23 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How is whole genome methylation interrogated?
    • How are methylation values commonly reported?
    • What preliminary R packages and data is necessary to begin methylation analysis?

    Objectives

    • Setting up the R environment and required packages
    • Create a sample table and define the variable of interest
    • Download the six publicly available sample data from GEO
    • Import the IDAT files into a minfi object

    Introduction

    Methylation in the human genome is known to be associated with development and disease. The Illumina Infinium methylation arrays are by far the most common way to interrogate methylation across the human genome. This workshop provides an easy and reproducible workflow using multiple packages for the analysis of methylation array data. Specifically, we demonstrate the steps involved in a typical differential methylation analysis pipeline including: quality control, filtering, normalization, data exploration and statistical testing for probe-wise differential methylation.

    DNA methylation, the addition of a methyl group to a CG dinucleotide of the DNA, is the most extensively studied epigenetic mark due to its role in both development and disease. Although DNA methylation can be measured in several ways, the epigenetics community has enthusiastically embraced the Illumina HumanMethylation450 (450k) array as a cost-effective way to assay methylation across the human genome. Illumina has increased the genomic coverage of the platform with their MethylationEPIC (850k) array, and more recently MethylationEPICv2 (935k) covering to >935,000 sites. As methylation arrays are likely to remain popular for measuring methylation for the foreseeable future, it is necessary to provide robust workflows for methylation array analysis.

    For each CpG, there are two measurements: a methylated intensity (denoted by 𝑀) and an unmethylated intensity (denoted by 𝑈). These intensity values can be used to determine the proportion of methylation at each CpG locus. Methylation levels are commonly reported as either beta values (𝛽=𝑀/(𝑀+𝑈)) or M-values (𝑀𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑢𝑒=𝑙𝑜𝑔2(𝑀/𝑈)).

    Beta values (proportion of methylation at a particular CpG site) are generally preferable for describing the level of methylation at a locus or for graphical presentation because percentage methylation is easily interpretable. M-values (log2 ratio of methylated to unmethylated signal intensity) are more appropriate for statistical testing. ## Load packages

    Complete the setup instructions first. Open RStudio and create a project using File > New Project > New Directory > New Project, or open your existing workshop project. Create an R script, and run the chunks below in order.

    Installing a package downloads it to your computer. Loading it with library() makes its functions available in the current session. Load the packages again whenever you restart R.

    R 

    # Data handling
library(dplyr)

# Methylation analysis and annotation
library(minfi)
library(GEOquery)
library(limma)
library(IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2anno.20a1.hg38)
library(IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2manifest)
library(AnnotationHub)
library(DMRcate)
library(missMethyl)

# Plotting
library(ComplexHeatmap)

    Load annotation data

    This is information that describes each CpG probe on the Illumina EPICv2 methylation array. It tells you where each probe is located in the genome and which genes or genomic features it is associated with.

    R 

    epic <- getAnnotation(IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2anno.20a1.hg38)
head(epic)

    Download data

    We use six EPICv2 arrays from GEO GSE240469: three technical replicates each of LNCaP and PrEC, all at 500 ng DNA input.

    • LNCaP is a prostate cancer cell line: cells grown in culture that model aspects of prostate cancer.
    • PrEC is a primary culture of normal prostate epithelial cells. It provides a non-cancer comparison, but is not matched normal tissue from the same patient.

    These data come from Peters et al. (2024), Characterisation and reproducibility of the HumanMethylationEPIC v2.0 BeadChip for DNA methylation profiling. The study evaluated the array’s performance, including reproducibility and the impact of DNA input, across cell cultures and tumour-derived samples. Our workshop uses only the six 500 ng prostate culture arrays.

    Because these are technical replicates of the same culture, we expect them to have similar methylation profiles and cluster together. Whilst methylation studies can be performed on cultured cells, it is more traditionally used for primary human tissue (e.g. tumour tissue).

    Create the sample table

    Each row describes one sample. Accession identifies the GEO sample, Name matches its filename label, and Type identifies the cell line to compare.

    R 

    # Create the sample table for IDAT downloads. Replace this table with your own sample information when using your own data.

targets <- data.frame(
  Accession = c(
    "GSM7698438",
    "GSM7698446",
    "GSM7698462",
    "GSM7698435",
    "GSM7698443",
    "GSM7698459"
  ),
  Name = c(
    "LNCAP_500_1",
    "LNCAP_500_2",
    "LNCAP_500_3",
    "PREC_500_1",
    "PREC_500_2",
    "PREC_500_3"
  ),
  Type = c("LNCaP", "LNCaP", "LNCaP", "PREC", "PREC", "PREC")
)

targets$Name2 <- paste(
  targets$Accession, targets$Name, sep = "_"
)

# Define the variable of interest and convert it to a factor.
variable.of.choice <- as.factor(targets$Type)

targets

    OUTPUT

3 GSM7698462 LNCAP_500_3 LNCaP GSM7698462_LNCAP_500_3
4 GSM7698435  PREC_500_1  PREC  GSM7698435_PREC_500_1

    Download the IDAT files

    The following chunk downloads the IDAT files for the six accessions in targets. Each sample is saved in its own accession-named folder within your current project directory.

    R 

    # Download only IDAT files for the selected tutorial samples.
gsmlist <- lapply(
  targets$Accession,
  GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles,
  makeDirectory = TRUE,
  baseDir = getwd(),
  filter_regex = "[.]idat([.]gz)?$"
)
names(gsmlist) <- targets$Accession

    Read in .idats

    Add the sample names and file paths to targets, preserving its sample order. Basename is the path to each file pair.

    R 

    # Link the sample information to the downloaded IDAT files.
targets$Sample <- targets$Name
targets$Basename <- file.path(
  getwd(), targets$Accession, targets$Name2
)

# Read in raw data from the red/green IDAT files.
rgSet <- read.metharray.exp(targets = targets)
sampleNames(rgSet) <- targets$Sample
rgSet@annotation <- c(
  array = "IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2",
  annotation = "20a1.hg38"
)
rgSet

    rgSet contains the raw intensities for the six samples. For your own data, set targets$Basename to your file paths and use the annotation matching your array type. Quality control, filtering and normalisation follow in the next episode. ## Save the input objects for reuse

    targets contains sample information; rgSet contains the raw measurements.

    R 

    dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(targets, "data/targets.rds")
saveRDS(rgSet, "data/rgSet.rds")
    Key Points
    • Raw Illumina methylation array data are stored in .idat files, with one red-channel and one green-channel file per sample.
    • The targets data frame holds the sample metadata, linking each sample’s name and cell-line group to its IDAT file paths.
    • read.metharray.exp(targets = targets) reads the raw intensities into rgSet, an RGChannelSet object, ready for quality control and preprocessing.

    Content from First steps: quality control, filtering, normalisation and basic visualisation

    Overview

    Questions

    • Why should we filter poor-quality samples and unreliable probes before differential methylation analysis?
    • What do detection p-values tell us about methylation array quality?
    • How can density and MDS plots help us identify unusual samples and unwanted variation?
    • How can biological differences, sample preparation and array batch affect methylation profiles?
    • Why do we normalise methylation array data, and why use functional normalisation for this comparison?
    • Why might we exclude probes based on chromosome location, SNPs or cross-reactivity?
    • How can we assess the effects of normalisation and filtering without mistaking biological differences for technical variation?

    Objectives

    • Calculate and interpret detection p-values to assess sample and probe quality
    • Apply sample and probe filters while keeping methylation measurements and sample metadata aligned
    • Create and interpret beta-value density plots and MDS plots to explore sample relationships and potential quality problems
    • Distinguish possible biological differences from variation associated with sample preparation or array batch
    • Perform functional normalisation and explain why it suits a cancer–normal comparison
    • Explain the rationale and limitations of chromosome, SNP and cross-reactivity filters
    • Compare plots before and after processing to assess changes in methylation distributions and sample relationships
    • Recognise when batch effects or confounding require further investigation beyond normalisation

    Quality control

    A detection p-value measures whether a probe’s signal can be distinguished from background. Smaller values support detectable signal.

    We calculate the detection p-values (detP) and examine their mean across probes for each sample to identify potentially failed samples. The Bioconductor methylation-array workflow uses a mean detection p-value cutoff of 0.05 for sample filtering. The red line marks a mean detection p-value of 0.05.

    The PDF report provides additional sample quality information.

    R 

    detP <- detectionP(rgSet)
head(detP)

    OUTPUT

cg25455143_BC11           0           0           0          0          0
cg25459778_BC11           0           0           0          0          0
cg25487775_BC11           0           0           0          0          0
cg25595446_BC11           0           0           0          0          0

    R 

    cols_type <- c(LNCaP = "#D55E00", PREC = "#0072B2")

barplot(
  colMeans(detP),
  col = cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)],
  las = 2,
  cex.names = 0.6,
  ylab = "Mean detection p-values",
  ylim = c(0, max(0.06, max(colMeans(detP), na.rm = TRUE)))
)
abline(h = 0.05, col = "red")
legend(
  "topright",
  legend = levels(factor(targets$Type)),
  fill = cols_type[levels(factor(targets$Type))],
  cex = 0.7,
  bg = "white"
)

    R 

    dir.create("data/figures", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
qcReport(
  rgSet,
  sampNames = targets$Sample,
  pdf = "data/figures/qcReport_combined_all_samples.pdf"
)

    OUTPUT 

    png
  2

    Filter poor quality samples

    Retain samples with a mean detection p-value below 0.05. Samples with a mean detection p-value at or above 0.05 are removed. Subset rgSet, targets and detP together so the sample information for the poor quality samples are removed together.

    R 

    keep <- colMeans(detP) < 0.05
rgSet <- rgSet[,keep]
rgSet

    Challenge

    Sample quality versus probe quality

    Why do we subset targets and detP when we remove a sample from rgSet? Could a sample pass the mean detection p-value filter but still contain failed probes?

    All three objects must describe the same samples in the same order. Otherwise, we could assign the wrong group to a sample or filter using another sample’s measurements. Yes: averaging can conceal individual failed probes, so we also apply a probe-level filter later.

    Explore sample identity with SNP control probes

    The EPIC array also contains 65 probes designed to target SNPs which can help investigate sample identity and possible mix-ups. SNP beta values reflect allele signals rather than CpG methylation levels. Here we plot a simple heatmap where rows represent SNP probes and columns represent samples. Samples with similar SNP profiles cluster together.

    R 

    snp_beta <- getSnpBeta(rgSet)
dim(snp_beta)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 65  6

    R 

    sample_annotation <- ComplexHeatmap::HeatmapAnnotation(
  Cell_line = targets$Type,
  col = list(Cell_line = cols_type)
)

ComplexHeatmap::draw(ComplexHeatmap::Heatmap(
  snp_beta,
  name = "SNP beta",
  col = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0, 0.5, 1), c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")),
  top_annotation = sample_annotation,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  cluster_columns = TRUE,
  show_row_names = FALSE,
  column_names_rot = 45
))

    Create a raw MethylSet and inspect outlier peaks

    preprocessRaw() converts the raw channels to methylated and unmethylated intensities. Beta values near zero indicate low methylation; values near one indicate high methylation.

    We investigate unusual density curves by counting peaks in each sample’s density curve and flagging samples with more than three peaks for visual inspection. This is a diagnostic heuristic: peak counts depend on smoothing and can reflect biology.

    R 

    mSetRaw <- preprocessRaw(rgSet)

densityPlot(getBeta(mSetRaw), main = "Raw", legend = FALSE)

    R 

    find_peaks <- function(x) {
  d <- density(x[!is.na(x)])
  d$x[c(FALSE, diff(diff(d$y) >= 0) < 0)]
}

all_peaks <- apply(getBeta(mSetRaw), 2, function(x) {
  find_peaks(x)
})
table(lengths(all_peaks) > 3)

    OUTPUT 

    
FALSE  TRUE
    2     4

    R 

    beta_mat <- as.matrix(getBeta(mSetRaw))
is_outlier <- lengths(all_peaks) > 3
peak_outlier_check <- factor(
  ifelse(is_outlier, "Outlier", "Non-outlier"),
  levels = c("Non-outlier", "Outlier")
)
densityPlot(
  beta_mat,
  sampGroups = peak_outlier_check,
  main = "Raw beta densities (outliers in red)",
  legend = FALSE,
  pal = c("grey70", "red")
)
legend(
  "top",
  legend = c("Non-outlier", "Outlier"),
  col = c("grey70", "red"),
  lty = 1,
  horiz = TRUE,
  bty = "n",
  inset = c(0, -0.02)
)

    Samples identified with outlier peaks have similar distribution to non-outliers. Hence visual inspection does not justify filtering out any samples.

    Normalisation

    Normalisation aims to reduce unwanted technical variation. We perform functional normalisation, then compare raw and normalised beta-value distributions.

    Callout

    Why use functional normalisation here?

    LNCaP cancer cells and PrEC normal prostate epithelial cells may have widespread biological methylation differences. We use preprocessFunnorm() because it uses control-probe information to adjust unwanted variation while aiming to preserve these global biological differences.

    In contrast, preprocessQuantile() assumes broadly comparable methylation distributions and is more appropriate when substantial global differences are not expected. This choice follows the minfi preprocessing guidance for cancer–normal comparisons; it is a starting guideline rather than a guarantee that one method is always best.

    Compare density plots, MDS and technical-replicate agreement after processing. The two cell types do not need identical density curves. Normalisation also does not automatically resolve batch effects or confounding.

    R 

    mSetFn <- preprocessFunnorm(rgSet)

layout(
  matrix(c(1, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3), 2, 3, byrow = TRUE),
  widths = c(1, 1, 0.3),
  heights = c(1, 1)
)
densityPlot(rgSet, sampGroups = targets$Type, main = "Raw", legend = FALSE, pal = cols_type[levels(factor(targets$Type))])
densityPlot(getBeta(mSetFn), sampGroups = targets$Type, main = "Normalised", legend = FALSE, pal = cols_type[levels(factor(targets$Type))])
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()

    Preliminary visualisation of data with MDS plot

    Multidimensional scaling (MDS) summarises similarities between samples using M-values. top=1000 and gene.selection="common" select the same 1,000 most variable probes across samples for the plot.

    The first pair of panels shows uncoloured samples and samples coloured by cell line. The next panels examine higher dimensions, coloured by cell line.

    R 

    par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(4,4,2,1), pty="s")
plotMDS(getM(mSetFn), top=1000, gene.selection="common", cex=0.9, pch = 19)

plotMDS(getM(mSetFn), top=1000, gene.selection="common",
        col=cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)], cex=0.9, pch = 19)

    R 

    par(mfrow=c(1,3), mar=c(4,4,2,1), pty="s")
plotMDS(getM(mSetFn), top=1000, gene.selection="common",
        col=cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)], dim=c(1,3), pch = 19)

plotMDS(getM(mSetFn), top=1000, gene.selection="common",
        col=cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)], dim=c(2,3), pch = 19)

plotMDS(getM(mSetFn), top=1000, gene.selection="common",
        col=cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)], dim=c(3,4), pch = 19)

    Look for grouping by cell line, agreement between replicates and isolated samples. These plots are exploratory; separation does not identify individual differentially methylated probes.

    Filter failed or poor quality probes

    When microarrays run, each probe measures a fluorescent intensity signal. To determine if a probe actually caught a biological signal or is just showing random machine noise, software calculates a detection p-value against a background noise distribution.

    The Bioconductor methylation-array workflow uses detection p-values below 0.01 for probe filtering. This means the signal is statistically different from background noise and the probe is kept. Probes are retained only when detection p-values are below 0.01 in every retained sample.

    R 

    # Ensure probes in same order
detP <- detP[match(featureNames(mSetFn), rownames(detP)), ]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(mSetFn), colnames(detP)))

keep <- rowSums(detP < 0.01) == ncol(mSetFn)
table(keep)

    OUTPUT 

    keep
 FALSE   TRUE
  5936 924139

    R 

    mSetFnFlt <- mSetFn[keep, ]
mSetFnFlt

    OUTPUT

    Filter sex chromosomes

    Remove probes annotated to chromosomes X and Y. This is to remove any sex variability in our analysis, not a statement that these measurements are unreliable. Keep them if your biological question concerns sex chromosomes and plan the analysis accordingly.

            epic$Name[epic$chr %in% c("chrX", "chrY")])

    Filter CpGs with SNPs

    Variants at the interrogated CpG or single-base extension site can affect the measurement. Use the matching array annotation to remove loci with annotated SNPs.

    R 

    mSetFnFlt <- mapToGenome(mSetFnFlt)
mSetFnFlt <- dropLociWithSnps(mSetFnFlt)

    Filter CpGs with potential cross-reactivity

    A probe is designed to measure methylation at a particular genomic location. If its sequence also binds elsewhere (cross-hybridisation, or cross-reactivity), its intensity may mix signals from multiple locations. A strong signal can still pass detection QC while representing the wrong or more than one locus, potentially misleading differential methylation results. These cross-reactive probes need to be filtered out.

    A manifest is a reference table describing the array’s probes, including probe identifiers, sequences and design information. The extended EPICv2 manifest from Peters et al. (2024) adds probe annotations, including predicted cross-hybridisation. See the EPICv2manifest reference manual for the extended table.

    We use AnnotationHub, a Bioconductor service for retrieving reference resources, to retrieve the extended EPICv2 manifest (AH116484). This table supplies extra filtering information beyond the epic genomic annotation loaded earlier.

    The CH_BLAT field flags predicted cross-hybridisation based on probe-sequence alignment using BLAT. We exclude entries marked "Y", matching their full EPICv2 probe IDs to our measurement rows. This is a prediction-based filter, not evidence that cross-hybridisation occurred in each sample.

    R 

    # Retrieve the reference table
ah <- AnnotationHub()

    R 

    epicv2_manifest <- ah[["AH116484"]]

    R 

    # Select IDs flagged for predicted cross-hybridisation
xReactiveProbes <- rownames(epicv2_manifest)[epicv2_manifest$CH_BLAT == "Y"]

# Keep measured probes whose IDs are absent from the flagged list
keep <- !(featureNames(mSetFnFlt) %in% xReactiveProbes)
table(keep)

    OUTPUT 

    keep
 FALSE   TRUE

    R 

    mSetFnFlt <- mSetFnFlt[keep, ]
mSetFnFlt

    Callout

    Alternative/additional workflows

    As an alternative to the separate SNP and cross-reactivity filters above, DMRcate::rmSNPandCH() filters a matrix of beta values or M-values. For example, start with the normalised data after detection filtering:

    R 

    betaFnFlt <- DMRcate::rmSNPandCH(betaFn)

    By default, rmSNPandCH() filters SNP-associated probes and removes cross-reactive probes (rmcrosshyb = TRUE). Sex-chromosome probes are retained by default; add rmXY = TRUE to exclude them too. Its criteria and annotation resources can differ from the separate dropLociWithSnps() and CH_BLAT filtering steps used here, so the retained probe sets need not be identical. See the DMRcate reference manual.

    EPICv2 includes multiple probes that map to the same CpG site. These are replicate probes within an array, distinct from the technical replicate samples in this lesson. Keeping multiple measurements per locus can give some sites extra weight in region analysis. The filters above remove unreliable probes but do not collapse replicate groups.

    Replicate handling is a separate optional step: options include averaging measurements or selecting a representative probe. In current DMRcate versions, cpg.annotate(..., arraytype = "EPICv2", epicv2Filter = "mean") handles replicate groups during annotation. Keep complete EPICv2 probe IDs until this step; removing their suffixes alone does not combine the measurements.

    For this EPICv2 dataset, average replicate M-values at each CpG position before saving; skip this optional step for older arrays.

    R 

    # Remove probes with non-finite M-values before DMRcate calculates variances.
mVals <- getM(mSetFnFlt)
keep <- rowSums(!is.finite(mVals)) == 0
table(keep)

    OUTPUT 

    keep
 FALSE   TRUE
     1 858894

    R 

    mSetFnFlt <- mSetFnFlt[keep, ]

# Collapse replicate probes by averaging measurements
epicv2CollapsedAnnotation <- DMRcate::cpg.annotate(
  datatype = "array",
  object = getM(mSetFnFlt),
  what = "M",
  arraytype = "EPICv2",
  epicv2Filter = "mean",
  epicv2Remap = FALSE,
  analysis.type = "variability"
)

# Extract beta values transformed from the averaged M-values.
averaged_beta <- epicv2CollapsedAnnotation@betas

# Translate DMRcate positions back to probe IDs
probe_ids <- featureNames(mSetFnFlt)
probe_annotation <- epic[match(probe_ids, epic$Name), ]
cpg_position <- paste(probe_annotation$chr, probe_annotation$pos, sep=":")
rownames(averaged_beta) <- probe_ids[match(rownames(averaged_beta), cpg_position)]

# Keep the saved object compatible with getM() and getBeta().
mSetFnFlt <- makeGenomicRatioSetFromMatrix(
  mat=averaged_beta, what="Beta",
  array="IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2", annotation="20a1.hg38"
)
mSetFnFlt

    Save files

    R 

    dir.create("data/processed", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(mSetFnFlt, file = "data/processed/normalised-filtered.rds")
saveRDS(targets, file = "data/processed/targets.rds")

    Re-examine MDS after filtering

    Plot the filtered M-values, to re-visualise the methylation data.

    R 

    par(mfrow=c(1,1), mar=c(4,4,2,1), pty="s")
plotMDS(getM(mSetFnFlt), top=1000, gene.selection="common",
        col = cols_type[as.character(targets$Type)], cex=0.8, pch=19)
legend("bottom", legend=names(cols_type), col = cols_type, pch = 19,
       cex=0.8, bg="white")

    Check whether replicates cluster together, whether cell lines separate, and whether any sample is unusual. The most variable probes can change after filtering, so the before- and after-filtering plots can be plotting different probes. An MDS plot is exploratory and does not identify differentially methylated probes.

    Challenge

    Interpret the plots

    1. What are some other variables in a given dataset that you would want to explore with MDS?
    2. What would you investigate before removing an isolated sample?
    1. Other variables that can contribute to differential methylation: sex, batch, age etc
    2. Check detection failures, raw intensities, sample labels, experimental records and known technical factors. An isolated point can also reflect genuine biology; a plot alone is not a sufficient exclusion rule.
    Key Points
    • Calculate detection p-values on raw data and inspect both sample and probe quality.
    • Keep metadata, detection p-values and methylation objects aligned by identifier.
    • Normalisation assumptions must fit the biological comparison.
    • Detection, chromosome, SNP and cross-reactivity filters address different questions.
    • Density and MDS plots help identify patterns worth investigating; they do not prove a batch effect or differential methylation.
    • Save processed objects and record filtering decisions for reproducible downstream analysis.

    Content from Differentially methylated probes with limma

    Last updated on 2026-10-23 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we compare methylation at individual probes between groups?
    • How do we define a design matrix and a contrast for limma?
    • How do we interpret and visualise differentially methylated probes?

    Objectives

    • Extract M-values and beta values from the filtered methylation data
    • Define a design matrix and contrast for LNCaP versus PrEC
    • Fit probe-wise models and identify differentially methylated probes with limma
    • Interpret effect direction, adjusted p-values and beta-value differences
    • Plot individual probes and cluster samples using the top-ranked probes

    A differentially methylated probe (DMP) measures a difference in methylation at an individual probe between the groups of interest. We use M-values for statistical testing and beta values to visualise methylation levels.

    Load filtered methylation data

    Start from the previously saved normalised and filtered objects. The annotation must match our EPICv2 array and hg38 genome build.

    R 

    library(minfi)
library(limma)
library(IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2anno.20a1.hg38)
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(dplyr)
library(missMethyl)

mSetFnFlt <- readRDS(file="data/processed/normalised-filtered.rds")
targets <- readRDS(file = "data/processed/targets.rds")
epic <- getAnnotation(IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICv2anno.20a1.hg38)

    Global M-values and beta values

    Here we look at the global M and Beta values across all probes. Beta values near zero indicate low methylation; values near one indicate high methylation. M-values are on a log-ratio scale. Inspect their distributions before fitting the model.

    R 

    cols_type <- c(LNCaP = "#D55E00", PREC = "#0072B2")

mVals <- getM(mSetFnFlt)
head(mVals)

    Define the design matrix and contrasts

    We compare LNCaP with PrEC. ~0+sampleType creates a column for each cell type, without an intercept; each coefficient represents that group’s mean M-value. Inspect the design to check that the sample labels are assigned correctly.

    R 

    sampleType <- factor(targets$Type)

design <- model.matrix(~0+sampleType, data=targets)
colnames(design) <- levels(sampleType)
design

    OUTPUT 

      LNCaP PREC
1     1    0
2     1    0
3     1    0
4     0    1
5     0    1
6     0    1
attr(,"assign")
[1] 1 1
attr(,"contrasts")
attr(,"contrasts")$sampleType
[1] "contr.treatment"
    Callout

    Technical replicates versus biological replicates

    For this example, we compare one prostate cancer cell line (LNCaP) with one normal prostate epithelial culture (PrEC), with three technical replicate arrays for each. These are repeated measurements of the same biological material, rather than three independent biological samples per group.

    In a typical research study, we would use biological replicates: e.g. tumours from different patients with the same disease type, in each comparison group. These samples capture biological variation between patients or tumours, which technical replicates alone cannot represent. Repeating measurements of one sample does not replace collecting independent biological samples.

    For your own study, define the groups using the biological question and account for the study design, including patient pairing where appropriate. Multiple tumours from the same patient are related samples and need that relationship accounted for in the analysis. See the Blocking and Correlation section of the limma User’s Guide to account for related samples using patient blocks and duplicateCorrelation().

    Fit models with limma

    lmFit() fits a linear model at each probe. The contrast LNCaP-PREC subtracts the PrEC mean M-value from the LNCaP mean M-value. contrasts.fit() calculates this comparison, and eBayes() moderates the variance estimates across probes.

    Positive coefficients indicate higher methylation in LNCaP; negative coefficients indicate higher methylation in PrEC. The summary counts probes with negative significant, non-significant and positive significant results at the default Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value threshold of 0.05 (conventional choice is false dicovery rate 5%).

    R 

    fit <- lmFit(mVals, design)
contMatrix <- makeContrasts(LNCaP-PREC,
                           levels=design)
contMatrix

    OUTPUT 

           Contrasts
Levels  LNCaP - PREC
  LNCaP            1
  PREC            -1

    R 

    fit2 <- contrasts.fit(fit, contMatrix)
fit2 <- eBayes(fit2)

# Differentially methylated CpGs at FDR < 0.05
summary(decideTests(fit2))

    OUTPUT 

           LNCaP - PREC
Down         298607
NotSig       284859
Up           269126

    Interpret and visualise differentially methylated probes

    We create a results table containing all tested probes, ranked by evidence for differential methylation.

    topTable() ranks probes by evidence for differential methylation. In the table:

    • logFC is the difference in mean M-values for LNCaP minus PrEC
    • P.Value is the unadjusted p-value for that probe
    • adj.P.Val accounts for testing many probes using Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment
    • B is the log-odds of differential methylation under the fitted model
    • deltaBeta is the mean beta value in LNCaP minus the mean beta value in PrEC; positive values indicate higher methylation in LNCaP (the magnitude of methylation change)

    We then plot the 4 top-ranked probes. These probes are only considered statistically significant if their adjusted p-values meet our FDR threshold.

    The four plots show the top-ranked probes, which may or may not pass the FDR threshold. Check the adjusted p-values before describing them as significant.

    R 

    # results table of top differentially methylated probes for this contrast
epicSub <- epic[match(rownames(mVals),epic$Name), ]
DMPs <- topTable(fit2, num=Inf, coef=1, genelist=epicSub)

# Mean beta-value difference: LNCaP minus PrEC
deltaBeta <- rowMeans(bVals[, sampleType == "LNCaP", drop=FALSE]) -
  rowMeans(bVals[, sampleType == "PREC", drop=FALSE])
DMPs$deltaBeta <- deltaBeta[rownames(DMPs)]
# head(DMPs)

# Plot the four top-ranked CpGs
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
for (cpg in rownames(DMPs)[1:4]) {
  plotCpg(bVals, cpg=cpg, pheno=targets$Type, ylab="Beta values")
}

    R 

    dir.create("data/output", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write.table(DMPs, file="data/output/DMPs_epicv2_LNCaP_vs_PREC.csv", sep=",", row.names=FALSE)

    We can also extract only the statistically significant probes, retaining their statistics, annotation and beta-value differences.

    R 

    sigDMPs <- DMPs[DMPs$adj.P.Val < 0.05, ]
nrow(sigDMPs)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 567733

    R 

    # head(sigDMPs)
    Challenge

    Interpret the contrast

    1. A probe has logFC = -2 and adj.P.Val = 0.01. Which cell type has higher methylation?
    2. Does this mean methylation differs by two percentage points?
    3. What would happen to the sign and significance if we used PREC-LNCaP?
    1. PrEC has higher mean M-values for this probe.
    2. No. logFC is an M-value difference. Inspect deltaBeta and the beta-value plot for an interpretable effect size.
    3. The coefficient and effect direction reverse. The two-sided p-values and adjusted p-values remain the same.

    Plot specific genes of interest

    We explore GSTP1 and APC, genes with documented promoter methylation in prostate cancer models. See the studies of GSTP1 in LNCaP and LNCaP versus PrEC methylation.

    We can plot the methylation profiles of specific genes of interest - To do this, we find any relevant probes relating to the target gene by searching the reference (epic dataframe) - Note: We are typically most interested in probes relating to the promoter region of genes. Therefore, for genes that have a large number of probes, you may choose to only focus on the probes relating to the promoter region. We can filter probes in this region by refining our search to CpG ‘islands’ that are typically located in or near promoter regions (this information can be found in the Relation_to_Island column). For a more precise search, we can also filter probes in the promoter region by refining our search to probes located within 200 base pairs (TSS200) and 1500 base pairs (TSS1500) upstream of the transcriptional start site (TSS) - both of which are typically considered parts of the promoter region (this information can be found in the UCSC_RefGene_Group column). You will need to play around with these parameters to suit your analysis of interest.

    R 

    # GSTP1 - search for related probes
applicable_probes <- as.data.frame(epicSub) %>%
  filter(grepl("\\bGSTP1\\b", UCSC_RefGene_Name))

applicable_probes %>%
  dplyr::select(chr, pos, strand, Name, Relation_to_Island,
                UCSC_RefGene_Group, UCSC_RefGene_Name)

geneMap <- c("cg07003745_TC21" = "APC",

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

for (probeID in names(geneMap)) {
  plotCpg(bVals, cpg=probeID, pheno=targets$Type,
          mainPrefix=paste(geneMap[probeID], "-"),
          ylab="Beta values")
}

    Hierarchical clustering of the top CpG probes

    We will use the top 100 most differentiated CpG sites (this can be changed depending on your preference). Rows in the heatmap represent probes and columns represent samples. The code uses Euclidean distances and Ward’s clustering method, as in the example.

    R 

    # extract top 100 DMPs
top_DMPs <- DMPs[1:100, ]

selected_bVals <- bVals[rownames(bVals) %in% rownames(top_DMPs), ]

# computing the distance matrix using Euclidean distance
dist_matrix <- dist(t(selected_bVals), method = "euclidean")

# Performing hierarchical clustering using Ward's method
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "ward.D2")

# Plot dendrogram
plot(hc, main = "Hierarchical Clustering of DMPs - LNCaP vs PrEC", sub = "", xlab = "", cex.lab = 0.75, cex.axis = 0.75, cex.main = 1)

    R 

    # Plot heatmap
sample_annotation <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  Cell_line = targets$Type,
  col = list(Cell_line = cols_type)
)

Heatmap(selected_bVals,
        top_annotation = sample_annotation,
        cluster_rows = TRUE,
        cluster_columns = TRUE,
        name = "Beta Value",
        column_title = "Hierarchical Clustering of Samples by Top 100 DMPs - LNCaP vs PrEC",
        row_title = "Top 100 CpG Sites",
        clustering_method_rows = "ward.D2",
        clustering_method_columns = "ward.D2",
        row_names_gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 6)
)

    Gene set enrichment and gene ontology testing

    We can ask whether genes associated with significant CpG probes are enriched for particular biological processes (GO terms) or KEGG pathways. gometh() accounts for differences in the number of probes associated with each gene. We use probes with adj.P.Val < 0.05, matching our false discovery rate of 5%. All tested probes will be used as the background.

    The bias plots show how the probability of identifying a significant CpG varies with the number of probes associated with a gene. In the enrichment tables, inspect FDR to assess significance after testing many gene sets; the top ten terms are not necessarily significant.

    Enrichment indicates that genes associated with differential methylation are overrepresented in a gene set. It does not establish that a pathway is activated or inhibited, or that gene expression has changed. This analysis combines probes with positive and negative methylation differences.

    This code requires a version of missMethyl that supports array.type="EPIC_V2". See the missMethyl vignette for details, including recommendations for handling EPICv2 replicate probes that measure the same CpG site. It is recommended that EPICv2 replicate probes are handelled before continuing with differential methylation analysis. Replicate probes in our dataset were collapsed in the previous lesson.

    R 

    # Extract significant probes at 5% FDR.
sigCpGs <- DMPs$Name[DMPs$adj.P.Val < 0.05]
sigCpGs[1:10]

    # Background: all probes tested in this comparison.
allCpGs <- DMPs$Name

    R 

    # GO enrichment analysis
gst <- gometh(sig.cpg=sigCpGs, all.cpg=allCpGs,
              array.type="EPIC_V2", collection="GO", plot.bias=TRUE)

    print(topGSA(gst, number=10))

    Key Points
    • Use M-values for probe-wise modelling and beta values to describe methylation levels.
    • The design encodes the groups; the contrast defines the comparison and effect direction.
    • Investigate genes of interest by searching the annotation and selecting probes relevant to the biological question, such as promoter-associated CpG-island probes.
    • Plot individual probes to compare methylation levels and variation within each group.
    • Use hierarchical clustering and an annotated heatmap of the top-ranked probes to visualise methylation patterns and sample relationships.
    • Explore GO and KEGG enrichment using significant probes and all tested probes as the background.
